clues: Affected untreated infants develop hypopigmentation, intellectual disability, and a characteristic mousy or musty body odor.
Tyrosine becomes an essential dietary amino acid in patients with this condition.
This autosomal recessive disorder is most commonly caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency.
Affected newborns present in the first week of life with poor feeding, dystonia, and sweet-smelling cerumen and urine.
Dietary management requires restricting leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
This disorder is caused by deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex.
Patients resemble those with Marfan syndrome, except their ocular lenses dislocate downward and inward and they have intellectual disability.
High-dose vitamin B6 supplementation helps about half of affected individuals.
This disorder is most commonly caused by cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency and carries a high risk of thromboembolism.
It is an inherited renal tubular transport defect rather than an enzymatic block.
Urinalysis shows characteristic hexagonal crystals, and patients develop recurrent radiopaque kidney stones.
It impairs reabsorption of cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine in the proximal tubule.

terms.sub: Organic Acidemias and Urea Cycle Defects
clues: Unlike all other defects in its pathway, it is inherited as an X-linked trait.
Affected male neonates present with severe hyperammonemia and elevated urinary orotic acid.
This enzyme deficiency prevents the condensation of carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline.
Symptoms appear within days of starting breast milk or standard infant formula, and affected neonates are prone to E. coli sepsis.
Removing lactose from the diet prevents liver failure and cataracts.
This autosomal recessive disorder is caused by galactose 1-phosphate uridylyltransferase deficiency.
Infants remain completely healthy while exclusively breastfed until fruit juices or sucrose are introduced.
Trapped phosphorylated sugar depletes hepatic inorganic phosphate and causes severe hypoglycemia and vomiting.
This autosomal recessive disorder is caused by aldolase B deficiency.
Unlike other glycogen storage diseases, the excess carbohydrate accumulates inside membrane-bound organelles rather than free in the cytosol.
Infants present with profound hypotonia, macroglossia, and massive cardiomegaly.
This Type II glycogen storage disease is caused by lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency.
Affected infants show developmental regression, hyperacusis, and a macular cherry-red spot without liver or spleen enlargement.
Onion-skin lysosomes accumulate inside central nervous system neurons.
This autosomal recessive sphingolipidosis is caused by hexosaminidase A deficiency.
It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and presents with pancytopenia, bone crises, and massive hepatosplenomegaly.
Bone marrow biopsy reveals macrophages with cytoplasm resembling crinkled tissue paper.
This disorder is caused by beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency.
Patients exhibit coarse facial features, gingival hyperplasia, and skeletal abnormalities from birth.
Newly synthesized acid hydrolases are mistakenly secreted into the blood instead of being delivered to their target organelle.
This mucolipidosis results from failure to phosphorylate mannose residues into mannose 6-phosphate in the Golgi apparatus.

terms.sub: Fatty Acid, Lipoprotein, Purine, and Heme Disorders
clues: It can present suddenly in infancy during a viral illness or prolonged overnight fast with hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
Urine organic acid analysis shows elevated C6 to C10 dicarboxylic acids.
This most common inborn error of fatty acid oxidation is caused by medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.
